# DISJOINT UNIONS AND FIXED-PARAMETER ALGORITHMS FOR CHROMATIC VILLAINY

Abstract. Chromatic villainy is the maximum, over rearrangements of optimal graph colorings, of the minimum Hamming distance to a proper coloring with the same color multiplicities. Weak villainy allows the repair to change these multiplicities. We give exact composition laws for disjoint unions and determine the eventual growth under repetition. Write _mG_ for the disjoint union of _m_ copies of _G_. For every graph _G_, with \(k=\chi(G)\), weak villainy satisfies _B_w(_mG_)=_mF<sub>k</sub>(G_) whenever _k|m_, where _F<sub>k</sub>(G_) is the maximum distance to a proper _k_-coloring over all assignments of _k_ color labels to vertices. Its bounded defect from _mF<sub>k</sub>(G_) is eventually periodic; we give an explicit stabilization bound and identify the least period, which divides _k_. For ordinary villainy, we obtain a computable rational slope \(\Lambda(G)\ge F_k(G)\) such that \(B(mG)=m\Lambda(G)+O_G(1)\), where the error is bounded independently of _m_ and eventually periodic, with a computable period and threshold. Consequently the difference between the two values is bounded exactly when \(\Lambda(G)=F_k(G)\), and otherwise grows linearly. The slope is determined by a finite optimization using at most _k_ source assignments. We also answer the unrestricted superadditivity questions negatively: for every _C\>_0, a connected graph can lose more than _C_ in weak villainy after union with a triangle, and some connected 3-chromatic graph _G_ satisfies \(B(G\sqcup G)<2B(G)-C\). Finally, both exact values on an _n_-vertex graph can be computed in time _f(B_w(_G_))(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>, without either value being supplied. Threshold recognition is fixed-parameter tractable as well.

### 1. Introduction

Chromatic villainy measures the cost of repairing a rearrangement of an optimal coloring. The cost counts vertices whose colors change. In the _villainy B(G_) of Clark et al. [2], the repair must preserve every color multiplicity; _weak villainy_<sub>w</sub>(_G_) permits different multiplicities on the same \(\chi(G)\)-color palette. Both parameters maximize the minimum repair distance over all such rearrangements. Thus \(0\le B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le B(G)\le|V(G)|\). A _word_ is any assignment of color labels to vertices, without requiring properness. Its _profile_ is the vector of its labeled color multiplicities; it is feasible if a proper coloring realizes it (Theorem 2.1). We call a rearranged source coloring a disturbance.

We study the behavior of these parameters under disjoint union and the complexity of recognizing graphs with a fixed value. Both questions were raised in the early literature; see [2, 14] and the account of Jahanbekam and Lin [12]. Clark et al. proved that weak villainy is superadditive under disjoint union when the summands have the same chromatic number. They proved the ordinary analogue under the additional assumption that every optimal coloring of one summand has equal-sized color classes. It was natural to ask whether these restrictions could be removed, and to determine when equality holds. On the algorithmic side, the classifications of graphs with villainy zero [2] and villainy two [12] give polynomial-time recognition in those cases. The complexity at other fixed values remained to be determined.

This paper continues our study in [13], where we determined odd-cycle profile radii, obtained complete multipartite formulas, and determined the extremal values at fixed order and chromatic number. Here we turn to disjoint unions and computation. The profile viewpoint remains central, but composition requires tracking transfers of color counts and, for ordinary repair, simultaneous responses to different target profiles. Our aim is to describe how global multiplicity constraints combine local repair costs, and to determine when those costs can be computed efficiently. For unions, we retain source profiles and _repair responses_, which record

## 1.1. Disjoint unions and profile composition.

The requirement that the global source profile be feasible couples the components. Although a disturbance preserves the total number of occurrences of each color, its restriction to a component need not have the profile of any proper coloring of that component. Similarly, an ordinary repair may transfer color multiplicities between components while preserving their global totals. When the chromatic numbers differ, one component also gains access to a larger palette. These features distinguish villainy from the unrestricted Hamming covering radius, the greatest distance of any word to a prescribed set of words. That radius is additive on Cartesian products of codes [3, Section II.C].

Our first results answer both unrestricted superadditivity questions negatively. For every real _C\>_0, there exists a connected graph _G_ such that<tbc>

\(B_\mathrm{w}(G\sqcup K_3)<B_\mathrm{w}(G)+B_\mathrm{w}(K_3)-C.\)

<tbc>Thus one summand in the weak counterexample can be a fixed triangle. For ordinary villainy, equal chromatic numbers do not suffice: for every real _C\>_0, there exists a connected graph _G_ with \(\chi(G)=3\) such that

\(B(G\sqcup G)<2B(G)-C.\)

Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 give explicit constructions.

To describe what replaces additivity, we keep track of source and target profiles. For weak repair, the relevant local information is the largest repair distance among words of each prescribed source profile, with the palette fixed in advance. Theorem 4.3 expresses the value on a union through these local radii. The formula separates the effect of changing the palette from that of transferring color counts between components. It gives an exact equality criterion in local profile data, including when the chromatic numbers differ.

Repeated copies admit a particularly simple weak-repair theorem. Let _mG_ denote the disjoint union of _m_ copies of _G_, put \(k=\chi(G)\), and let _F<sub>k</sub>(G_) be the _k_-fixing number of Garnero et al. [9]: the maximum distance to a proper _k_-coloring over _all_ source words on that palette. If _m=qk+r_ with \(0\le r<k\), Theorem 4.5 proves<tbc>

\(0\le mF_k(G)-B_\mathrm{w}(mG)\le r\big(F_k(G)-B_\mathrm{w}(G)\big).\)

<tbc>In particular, _B_<sub>w</sub>(_mG_)=_mF<sub>k</sub>(G_) whenever _k_ divides _m_, and _B_<sub>w</sub>(_mG)/m_ converges to _F<sub>k</sub>(G_). Moreover, weak villainy is additive over every repetition if and only if _B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_)=_F<sub>k</sub>(G_); it suffices to test the union of _k_ copies. The proof balances the color counts of a worst unrestricted source by cyclically relabeling its colors on _k_ copies. Theorem 4.6 makes the eventual behavior effective. For _n_=|_V(G_)| and \(k\ge 2\), put<tbc>

\(M=\big(2(k-1)n+1\big)^{k-1},N=(k-1)M.\)

<tbc>For every \(m\ge N\), the defect _mF<sub>k</sub>(G_)-_B_<sub>w</sub>(_mG_) is periodic. Its least period is

\(h=\mathrm{gcd}\{\ell\ge 1:B_\mathrm{w}(\ell G)=\ell F_k(G)\},h|k,\)

and the gcd can be computed using only \(\ell\le M\). Beyond _N_, the fixing-number bound is attained exactly when _h|m_. These weak-repair results hold on any fixed palette of size at least \(\chi(G)\).

Ordinary repair requires more information. A single disturbed coloring has a repair cost for each possible target profile, and these costs must be retained together. Maximizing each coordinate separately can combine costs that no single disturbance realizes. We therefore use the full response functions and discard only those bounded above at every target profile by another realizable response. To combine two responses, we minimize the sum of their costs over all splits of the target profile. This operation, called min-plus convolution in Theorem 4.8, gives Theorem 4.9. The resulting equality tests are finite criteria in component data; they do not constitute a structural classification of all equality pairs.

<tbc>The response description also yields a general repetition theorem for ordinary villainy. Theorem 4.11 gives a computable rational number \(\Lambda(G)\ge F_k(G)\) such that

\(B(mG)=m\Lambda(G)+O_G(1).\)

Here _O<sub>G</sub>_(1) denotes an error bounded by a constant depending only on _G_. The slope comes from an optimization that allows fractional proportions of copies to receive each source and target coloring, as defined in (4.15). Its maximum is attained by a distribution using at most _k_ source words. Moreover, \(B(mG)-m\Lambda(G)\) is eventually periodic, with a computable period and threshold. Thus Theorem 4.12 determines the possible growth of the difference between the repair rules: it is bounded precisely when \(\Lambda(G)=F_k(G)\), in which case it is eventually periodic; otherwise it grows linearly.

### 1.2. Fixed-parameter recognition.

Our algorithmic result computes both exact parameters using the potentially smaller weak villainy as parameter. Theorem 5.1 gives running time _h(B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_))(_n_+1)_<sup>c</sup>_, where _h_ is computable and _c_ is an absolute constant, without either value being supplied. Given an integer \(t\ge 0\), it also computes the two truncated values

\(min\{B(G),t+1\}\text{and}min\{B_\mathrm{w}(G),t+1\}\)

in time _f(t_)(_n_+1)_<sup>c</sup>_ for a computable function _f_. Thus both equality recognition, deciding whether a parameter equals _t_, and threshold recognition, deciding whether it is at most _t_, are fixed-parameter tractable in _t_: the polynomial exponent in the input size is independent of _t_. They are polynomial-time problems at every fixed value. In particular, unless P=NP, there is no fixed value at which villainy recognition is NP-complete.

The structural input is a matching bound. If \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le t\), then either _G_ has a vertex cover of size at most 2_t_, or \(\chi(G)\ge n-2t\) and the complement of _G_ has a vertex cover of size at most 4_t_. The same conclusion holds when \(B(G)\le t\). The proof groups vertices outside these covers by their neighborhoods and retains only source profiles realized by optimal proper colorings. In the small-cover case, a bounded-length formula with variables for the type sizes permits elimination of its quantified variables before the input multiplicities are substituted. In the complement-cover case, symmetries that fix the source coloring remove the need to enumerate singleton color names individually. The polynomial exponent is independent of _t_; the proof does not give a practical bound on the function _f_.

### 1.3. Related repair problems and organization.

Garnero et al. [9] study repair of an arbitrary given coloring and the fixing number used above. De Biasi and Lauri [5] consider a source promised to be a rearrangement of an optimal coloring. Their _r_-Fix-Promise problem is an individual weak-repair instance; their swap problem uses the number of color exchanges as cost. Our recognition problem quantifies over every admissible disturbance.

Count-aware component optimization also appears in the two-color repair algorithm of Fellows et al. [7]. It chooses orientations of bipartite components for one given source, subject to total color counts and a swap budget. For villainy, one must additionally retain jointly realizable responses before taking the worst-source maximum.

Finally, endpoint Hamming distance differs from proper-coloring reconfiguration [1, 8], where every intermediate coloring must be proper. Ordinary villainy constrains only the initial and final color multiplicities.

Section 2 fixes the notation and definitions. Section 3 gives the counterexamples to superadditivity. Section 4 develops the profile composition laws and the repeated-copy theorem. Section 5 proves fixed-parameter recognition, and Section 6 discusses further questions.

## 2. Color profiles and repair distances

All graphs are finite and simple. Unless otherwise stated, a graph _G_ is nonempty, has order _n_, and has chromatic number _k_. We use a fixed set C of _k_ labeled colors.

**Definition 2.1** (Words and profiles)**.** A _word_ on _G_ is a map \(w:V(G)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\), with no properness assumption. Its _profile_ is the vector \(\mathbf{m}(w)=(m_X(w))_{X\in\mathcal{C}}\), where _mX(w_)=|_w_-1(_X_)|. Bold letters denote vectors. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise, **e**_X_ is a coordinate unit vector, and **1** is an all-one vector of the required dimension. Write P(_G_) for the proper colorings with palette C. Since \(|\mathcal{C}|=\chi(G)\), each such coloring uses every color. A profile **m** is _feasible_ if it occurs in P(_G_). For a feasible profile, put \(\mathcal{W}_\mathbf{m}(G)=\{w:V(G)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}:\mathbf{m}(w)=\mathbf{m}\},\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{m}(G)=\mathcal{W}_\mathbf{m}(G)\cap\mathcal{P}(G).\) We omit _G_ from W**m**(_G_) when the vertex set is clear. Every word in W**m**(_G_) is a rearrangement of every proper coloring with that profile. We call such a word an _admissible disturbance_; equivalently, its profile is feasible. The Hamming distance and the number of agreements are \(d_\mathrm{H}(w,y)=|\{v:w(v)\neq y(v)\}|,\mathrm{agr}(w,y)=n-d_\mathrm{H}(w,y).\) The cost therefore counts changed vertices; exchanging two different colors on two vertices has cost two. **Definition 2.2** (Repair radii and villainy)**.** The repair radius of a profile and its weak counterpart are \(R_G(\mathbf{m})=\mathrm{max}_{w\in\mathcal{W}_\mathbf{m}(G)}\mathrm{min}_{y\in\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{m}(G)}d_\mathrm{H}(w,y),\)
\(R_G^\mathrm{w}(\mathbf{m})=\mathrm{max}_{w\in\mathcal{W}_\mathbf{m}(G)}\mathrm{min}_{y\in\mathcal{P}(G)}d_\mathrm{H}(w,y).\) With the terminology of Clark et al. \[2\], \(B(G)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{m}\text{feasible}}R_G(\mathbf{m}),B_\mathrm{w}(G)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{m}\text{feasible}}R_G^\mathrm{w}(\mathbf{m}).\) Both parameters are zero on the empty graph by convention. The inclusion of the two target sets gives \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le B(G)\). In particular, the weak target may change the profile, but it still uses the same palette of \(\chi(G)\) colors. A simultaneous permutation of the color labels in the source and target preserves distances and all profile conditions. We write \[_k_\]={1_,...,k_}. For sets of vectors _A,B_, their sum is \(A+B=\{\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}:\mathbf{a}\in A,\mathbf{b}\in B\}\). The graph _mG_ is the disjoint union of _m_ vertex-disjoint copies of _G_. ## 3. Counterexamples to superadditivity Clark et al. \[2, Propositions 3.7 and 3.8\] proved \(B_\mathrm{w}(G\sqcup H)\ge B_\mathrm{w}(G)+B_\mathrm{w}(H)\text{when}\chi(G)=\chi(H),\) (3.1) and its ordinary analogue when, in addition, every optimal coloring of one summand has equal-sized color classes. We show that the unrestricted inequalities fail by an arbitrarily large amount, even for connected summands. **Theorem 3.1.** _For every real C\>_0_, there exists a connected graph G such that_ \(B_\mathrm{w}(G\sqcup K_3)_Proof._ For a positive integer _s_, let _Ts_ consist of an edge _uv_ with 3_s_ leaves adjoined to each endpoint. Both bipartition classes have size 3_s_+1. The connected bipartite formula \[2, Proposition 3.3\] gives \(B_\mathrm{w}(T_s)=2\left\lfloor\frac{3s+1}{2}\right\rfloor,B_\mathrm{w}(K_3)=0.\) We show that \(B_\mathrm{w}(T_s\sqcup K_3)\le 2s+3\).

<tbc>The union has chromatic number three. For any three-color source _w_, let _N<sub>u</sub>(i),N<sub>v</sub>(i_) count the leaves of color _i_ at the two centers. Repairing the center colors to distinct labels _i,j_ has minimum tree cost

\(N_u(i)+N_v(j)+\mathbf{1}_{\{w(u)\neq i\}}+\mathbf{1}_{\{w(v)\neq j\}}.\)

Its average over the six ordered pairs is 2_s_+4/3. Some integer cost is therefore at most 2_s_+1. The triangle needs at most two changes, giving the required upper bound.

It follows that

\(B_\mathrm{w}(T_s)+B_\mathrm{w}(K_3)-B_\mathrm{w}(T_s\sqcup K_3)\ge 2\left\lfloor\frac{3s+1}{2}\right\rfloor-(2s+3)\ge s-3.\)

Choosing an integer _s\>C_+3 proves the stated strict inequality. □

For the ordinary parameter, the chromatic numbers can be equal and the two connected summands can even be isomorphic. We use the following general observation about a feasible profile **p** on _N_ vertices. If two proper targets of that profile have disjoint color-_X_ classes of size _p<sub>X</sub>_, then every source of profile **p** agrees with one of them on at least

\(\mathrm{max}\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{3p_X-N}{2}\right\rceil\right\}\) (3.2)

vertices. Indeed, the source _X_-set has size _p<sub>X</sub>_, and its intersection with the union of the two target _X_-sets has size at least 3_p<sub>X</sub>-N_. One of the two intersections has at least half that size.

**Theorem 3.2.** _For every real C\>_0_, there exists a connected graph G with_ \(\chi(G)=3\) _such that_

\(B(G\sqcup G)<2B(G)-C.\)

_Here the union consists of two vertex-disjoint copies of G._

_Proof._ For each positive integer _t_, take

\(J_t=\overline{K_{5t}}\vee\left(K_{t,2t}\sqcup K_{t,3t}\right),\)

where the join adds every edge between its two arguments. This is a connected graph of order 12_t_ and chromatic number three. Denote its five independent vertex sets by _S,L_<sub>1</sub>_,R_<sub>1</sub>_,L_<sub>2</sub>_,R_<sub>2</sub>, of respective sizes 5_t,t,_2_t,t,_3_t_. The set _S_ is joined to all four other sets, and the remaining edges are those between _L<sub>i</sub>_ and _R<sub>i</sub>_ for _i_=1,2.

In a proper three-coloring, the bipartite remainder requires two colors, so _S_ must use only the third. Each of its two connected components then has its two possible binary colorings. The possible unordered profiles on _J<sub>t</sub>_ are precisely _t_(2,5,5) and _t_(3,4,5). The labeled profile (3_t,_4_t,_5_t_) has a unique proper realization: _C_ occupies _S_, _A_ occupies \(R_1\cup L_2\), and _B_ occupies \(L_1\cup R_2\). A source with this profile and no agreement is described by the matrix

\(t\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
0 & 2 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 4 \\
3 & 2 & 0
\end{array}\right),\)

whose rows are these target classes and whose columns count the source colors. Its row and column sums are (3_t,_4_t,_5_t_), and its diagonal vanishes. Hence _B(J<sub>t</sub>_)=12_t_.

Adding two permutations of the possible profiles gives exactly the following sorted profiles on 2_J<sub>t</sub>_, divided by _t_:

\((4,10,10),(5,9,10),(6,8,10),(6,9,9),(7,7,10),(7,8,9),(8,8,8).\)

For clarity, adding two copies of (2,5,5) gives the first or fifth; mixing the two types gives the second, third, or sixth; adding two copies of (3,4,5) gives the third through seventh. In every unbalanced case the table supplies two targets with disjoint _C_-classes. Each five-letter word assigns colors to (_S,L_<sub>1</sub>_,R_<sub>1</sub>_,L_<sub>2</sub>_,R_<sub>2</sub>) in one copy, and the separator distinguishes the two copies.

<tbc>Every word is proper: its first letter differs from the other four, its second differs from its third, and its fourth differs from its fifth. Weighted letter counts verify each profile. In no position do both targets have _C_, so their _C_-classes are disjoint.

Here _N_=24_t_ and \(p_C\ge 9t\). By (3.2), every source of an unbalanced profile has a repair retaining at least \(\lceil 3t/2\rceil\) vertices. For the balanced profile (8_t,_8_t,_8_t_), the three cyclic relabelings of any proper target still have that profile and together agree once at every vertex. Some target therefore retains at least 8_t_ vertices. Consequently

\(B(2J_t)\le 24t-\left\lceil\frac{3t}{2}\right\rceil,2B(J_t)-B(2J_t)\ge\left\lceil\frac{3t}{2}\right\rceil.\)

Choose an integer _t\>_2_C/_3. Then \(\lceil 3t/2\rceil>C\), which gives the stated strict inequality. The upper bound on _B_(2_J<sub>t</sub>_) is all that is needed here; no exact value for it is asserted. □

## 4. Profile composition and repeated unions

The counterexamples in Section 3 show the effect of permitting color counts to move between components. We now retain the local profile data and derive exact composition laws. For repeated copies, these laws give eventual linear growth with periodic corrections under both repair rules. Weak repair has the explicit slope _F<sub>k</sub>(G_); ordinary repair has a rational slope described by a finite fractional optimization.

### 4.1. Weak repair and transfer of color counts.

To analyze arbitrary summands, their colorings must first be expressed in a common palette.

**Definition 4.1** (Common-palette radii)**.** Fix \(k\ge\chi(J)\), and let P_<sub>k</sub>(J_) be the set of proper maps from _V(J_) to \[_k_\]. These maps may leave some labels unused. Write

\(\mathcal{A}_k(J)=\left\{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^k:\sum_{i=1}^ka_i=|V(J)|\right\},\mathcal{M}_k(J)=\{\mathbf{m}(y):y\in\mathcal{P}_k(J)\}.\)

Thus A_<sub>k</sub>(J_) contains all source profiles, whereas M_<sub>k</sub>(J_) contains the profiles realized by proper colorings. The distinction matters even when \(k=\chi(J)\): a source restricted to one summand of a union need not have a feasible profile on that summand.

For every \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{A}_k(J)\), define<tbc>

\(\rho_{J,k}(\mathbf{a})=\mathrm{max}_{w:V(J)\rightarrow[k]}\mathrm{min}_{y\in\mathcal{P}_k(J)}d_\mathrm{H}(w,y).\)

<tbc>We shall use the two maxima

\(\beta_k(J)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}_k(J)}\rho_{J,k}(\mathbf{p}),F_k(J)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{A}_k(J)}\rho_{J,k}(\mathbf{a}).\) (4.1)

The first is weak villainy with the fixed palette \[_k_\]; in particular, \(\beta_{\chi(J)}(J)=B_\mathrm{w}(J)\). The second is the _k_-fixing number studied by Garnero et al. \[9\], in which the source coloring is unrestricted. Put

\(\varepsilon_k(J)=F_k(J)-\beta_k(J)\ge 0.\)

This difference measures how much is lost by requiring the source profile to be feasible.

<tbc>**Definition 4.2** (Transfer surplus)**.** For an integral vector \(\unknown\) whose coordinates sum to zero, define the _transfer surplus_

\(\Delta_{J,k}(\unknown)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}_k(J)\mathbf{p}+\unknown\ge\mathbf{0}}\rho_{J,k}(\mathbf{p}+\unknown)-\beta_k(J).\) (4.2)

An empty maximum has value \(-\infty\). The vector \(\unknown\) records a change in the local color counts relative to a proper coloring. Its coordinates can have both signs, although their sum is zero because the order of the summand is unchanged. For a union, this change must be offset by \(-\unknown\) on the other summand.

**Theorem 4.3.** _Let_ \(k\ge\mathrm{max}\{\chi(G),\chi(H)\}\)_, and put_<tbc>

\(T_k(G,H)=\mathrm{max}_\unknown\big(\Delta_{G,k}(\unknown)+\Delta_{H,k}(-\unknown)\big).\)

<tbc>_Then_<tbc>

\(\beta_k(G\sqcup H)=\beta_k(G)+\beta_k(H)+T_k(G,H),\) (4.3)

<tbc>_where_<tbc>

\(0\le T_k(G,H)\le\varepsilon_k(G)+\varepsilon_k(H).\) (4.4)

<tbc>_Proof._ A proper coloring of \(G\sqcup H\) is exactly a pair of local proper colorings, and hence<tbc>

\(\mathcal{M}_k(G\sqcup H)=\mathcal{M}_k(G)+\mathcal{M}_k(H).\)

<tbc>For fixed local source words, the two weak repairs are independent and their costs add. Maximizing over sources of prescribed local profiles therefore gives<tbc>

\(\beta_k(G\sqcup H)=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{A}_k(G),\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}_k(H)\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{M}_k(G)+\mathcal{M}_k(H)}\big(\rho_{G,k}(\mathbf{a})+\rho_{H,k}(\mathbf{c})\big).\) (4.5)

<tbc>For every admitted pair **a**,**c**, choose proper profiles **p**,**q** with **p**+**q**+**c**. Then

\(\unknown=\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{c}\)

has coordinate sum zero. Conversely, proper profiles **p**,**q** and a vector \(\unknown\) for which \(\mathbf{p}+\unknown\) and \(\mathbf{q}-\unknown\) are nonnegative determine an admitted source pair. For fixed \(\unknown\), the choices of **p** and **q** are independent. Substitution into (4.5) and separate maximization over these two profiles prove (4.3).

The zero transfer satisfies \(\Delta_{J,k}(\mathbf{0})=0\), so \(T_k(G,H)\ge 0\). Also \(\rho_{J,k}(\mathbf{p}+\unknown)\le F_k(J)\), which bounds each surplus by \(\varepsilon_k(J)\) and proves the upper bound in (4.4). □

The theorem identifies two distinct effects in the original superadditivity question. A common palette changes the individual weak-villainy values to \(\beta_k(G)\) and \(\beta_k(H)\). Relative to these common-palette values, transferring color counts can only increase the worst repair cost, and its entire contribution is _T<sub>k</sub>(G,H_).

**Corollary 4.4.** _If_ \(\chi(G)=\chi(H)=k\)_, then_<tbc>

\(B_\mathrm{w}(G\sqcup H)=B_\mathrm{w}(G)+B_\mathrm{w}(H)\)

<tbc>_if and only if_

\(\Delta_{G,k}(\unknown)+\Delta_{H,k}(-\unknown)\le 0\text{\textit{for every}}\unknown.\) (4.6)

_In particular, equality holds if F<sub>k</sub>(G_)=_B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_) _and F<sub>k</sub>(H_)=_B_<sub>w</sub>(_H)._

_For arbitrary G,H, set_ \(k=\mathrm{max}\{\chi(G),\chi(H)\}\) _and_<tbc>

\(\Gamma_k(G,H)=B_\mathrm{w}(G)+B_\mathrm{w}(H)-\beta_k(G)-\beta_k(H).\)

<tbc>_Then_

\(B_\mathrm{w}(G\sqcup H)-B_\mathrm{w}(G)-B_\mathrm{w}(H)=T_k(G,H)-\Gamma_k(G,H).\) (4.7)

_Consequently superadditivity holds if and only if_ \(T_k(G,H)\ge\Gamma_k(G,H)\)_, and equality holds if and only if_ \(T_k(G,H)=\Gamma_k(G,H)\).

<tbc>_Proof._ At equal chromatic numbers the palette correction is zero, and the maximum defining _T<sub>k</sub>_ already contains the zero transfer. Thus _T<sub>k</sub>_=0 is equivalent to (4.6). The sufficient condition follows from (4.4). For unequal chromatic numbers, subtract the two intrinsic weak-villainy values from (4.3). □

These criteria use local profile radii and remain valid for every graph pair. The correction \(\Gamma_k(G,H)\) is kept signed; the argument does not require an assumption about how the feasible- source maximum changes when additional colors are made available.

## 4.2. Repeated copies and the fixing number.

The unrestricted maximum _F<sub>k</sub>(G_) may be attained by a word whose profile is not feasible. Taking several copies of the graph permits such a word to be balanced across the palette. This gives an exact relation between weak villainy and the fixing number.

**Theorem 4.5.** _Fix an integer_ \(k\ge max\{1,\chi(G)\}\)_, and write m=qk+r, where_ \(q\ge 0\) _and_ \(0\le r<k\)_. Then_<tbc>

\(0\le mF_k(G)-\beta_k(mG)\le r\big(F_k(G)-\beta_k(G)\big).\) (4.8)

<tbc>_In particular,_<tbc>

\(\beta_k(mG)=mF_k(G)\text{\textit{whenever}}k|m,\) (4.9)

<tbc>_and_

\(lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\beta_k(mG)}{m}=F_k(G).\) (4.10)

_Proof._ Every source on _mG_ can be weakly repaired one copy at a time, each at cost at most _F<sub>k</sub>(G_). This proves the upper bound \(\beta_k(mG)\le mF_k(G)\).

Let _w_ be a word on _G_ at distance _F<sub>k</sub>(G_) from P_<sub>k</sub>(G_), and let \(\pi\) be a cyclic permutation of all _k_ color labels. On _k_ copies of _G_, use the sources

\(w,\pi\circ w,\dots,\pi^{k-1}\circ w.\)

If _G_ has _n_ vertices, their total profile is (_n,...,n_): the _k_ copies of every vertex receive every label once. This profile is feasible. Indeed, starting with any proper [_k_]-coloring _y_ of _G_, its _k_ cyclic relabelings give a proper coloring of _kG_ with the same total profile. Relabeling preserves distances to the proper-coloring set, so each of the _k_ sources still requires _F<sub>k</sub>(G_) changes in a weak repair. The repairs on distinct copies are independent. Thus this admitted source on _kG_ requires exactly _kF<sub>k</sub>(G_) changes.

Repeating the construction gives _qk_ copies with cost _qkF<sub>k</sub>(G_). On each of the remaining _r_ copies, use a feasible source attaining \(\beta_k(G)\). The resulting total profile is feasible, since every block and each remaining copy has a feasible profile. Its weak repair cost is

\(qkF_k(G)+r\beta_k(G).\)

Combining this lower bound with the upper bound proves (4.8). The exact formula when _r_=0 follows immediately, and the error in (4.8) is bounded independently of _m_, proving (4.10). □

When \(k=\chi(G)\), the common-palette quantities in this theorem are the intrinsic weak-villainy values.

The error in equation (4.8) eventually repeats. The following result gives an explicit stabilization bound and identifies its least period from the repetitions attaining the fixing- number bound.

## 4.3. Count-preserving repairs and response functions.

For ordinary villainy, the target profiles on the summands are coupled by their prescribed sum. We retain the common palette of _k_ colors and the profile sets A_<sub>k</sub>(J),_M_<sub>k</sub>(J_) introduced in Theorem 4.1. Local source profiles range over A_<sub>k</sub>(J_), even when they are not proper profiles.

**Definition 4.8** (Repair responses)**.** The _response function_ of a word \(w:V(J)\rightarrow[k]\) of profile **a** is<tbc>

\(f_w(\mathbf{p})=min_{y\in\mathcal{P}_k(J)\mathbf{m}(y)=\mathbf{p}}d_\mathrm{H}(w,y)(\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}_k(J)).\)

<tbc>Here all colorings and words use the common palette; a proper coloring of a summand need not use every color. Extend _f<sub>w</sub>_ by \(+\infty\) outside M_<sub>k</sub>(J_). Write

\(\mathcal{R}_k(J,\mathbf{a})=\mathrm{Max}\{f_w:\mathbf{m}(w)=\mathbf{a}\},\)

where Max retains the coordinatewise maximal functions and removes duplicates. Thus a response is discarded if another realizable response is at least as large at every target profile and larger at some profile. The resulting family is an _antichain_: no two distinct remaining responses are comparable coordinatewise. It records the possible tradeoffs between target profiles without retaining the source words themselves.

For two response functions define their min-plus convolution by

\((f\star g)(\mathbf{p})=min_{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}}\big(f(\mathbf{u})+g(\mathbf{v})\big).\)

The profiles where its value is finite are exactly M_<sub>k</sub>(G_)+M_<sub>k</sub>(H_) when _f,g_ are responses on _G,H_, respectively. For sets of responses, put \(\mathcal{U}\star\mathcal{V}=\{f\star g:f\in\mathcal{U},g\in\mathcal{V}\}\).

**Theorem 4.9.** _For every_ \(k\ge max\{\chi(G),\chi(H)\}\) _and every source profile_ **a** _on_ \(G\sqcup H\), \(\mathcal{R}_k(G\sqcup H,\mathbf{a})=Max\bigcup_{\alpha+\beta=\mathbf{a}}\big(\mathcal{R}_k(G,\alpha)\star\mathcal{R}_k(H,\beta)\big),\) (4.12) _where the union ranges over_ \(\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_k(G)\) _and_ \(\beta\in\mathcal{A}_k(H)\)_. This composition is associative and commutative._ _Proof._ A source word on the union restricts to words _w,z_ on the two summands. At a fixed target profile **p**, any proper repair has local target profiles **u**,**v** with **u**+**v**=**p**. Once these profiles are fixed, the two repairs are independent and their distances add. The union response is therefore exactly _fw⋆fz_. Conversely, any pair of local response functions can be realized simultaneously by choosing its two source words independently. This proves (4.12) before dominated responses are removed. Convolution is monotone in each argument: if \(f\le f'\) and \(g\le g'\), then \(f\star g\le f'\star g'\). Replacing a discarded local response by a maximal one can consequently only increase the resulting response. Pruning the local lists thus leaves the union’s maximal responses unchanged. Associativity and commutativity follow from those of min-plus convolution, and the same monotonicity permits pruning at every intermediate composition. □ This theorem is a reduction to finite local data; it does not assert that the response antichains are always small. When \(k=\chi(J)\), ordinary villainy is recovered from their diagonal entries: \(B(J)=max_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{M}_k(J)}max_{f\in\mathcal{R}_k(J,\mathbf{a})}f(\mathbf{a}).\) (4.13) The antichain is a singleton whenever one source attains every coordinatewise maximum simultaneously. The common extremizer in \[13, Theorem 3.15\] gives \(\mathcal{R}_3(C_{2r+1},\mathbf{a})=\{f_\mathbf{a}\},\)
\(f_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{p})=2r+1-\sum_{X\in[3]}min\{p_X,\lceil a_X/2\rceil\}(\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}_3(C_{2r+1}))\) for every source profile **a**, including infeasible ones: the same cyclic word, with all occurrences of each color consecutive, attains the displayed value at every target profile. Thus these directed radii supply the complete local response data needed for composition. In general, however, it is essential to retain the antichain, rather than merely the largest value in each coordinate. For example, on _P_3=_K_1,2 with two colors, order the target profiles by their _A_-counts 1,2. Sources with one _A_ have responses (0,3) and (2,1), according as _A_ occupies the center or a leaf. Sources with two _A_’s have responses (3,0) and (1,2). For two copies and the source split 1+2, the greatest convolution value at total _A_-count three is two. Taking coordinatewise maxima first instead gives \(min\{2+2,3+3\}=4.\) Indeed, the actual radius of profile (3,3) on 2_P_3 is two: its two proper targets are complementary, their distances from a same-profile source are even and sum to six, and a source constant on each copy attains two. Thus the outer maximum over disturbances cannot in general be interchanged with the minimum over target profiles. The response functions also give an exact criterion for equality under disjoint union. For an integer _j_, put \(\mathcal{L}_f(j)=\{\mathbf{p}:f(\mathbf{p})\le j\},\mathcal{K}_L(f,g)=\bigcup_{j=0}^L\big(\mathcal{L}_f(j)+\mathcal{L}_g(L-j)\big),\) with \(\mathcal{L}_f(j)=\varnothing\) for _j\<_0 and \(\mathcal{K}_{-1}(f,g)=\varnothing\). **Proposition 4.10.** _Set_ \(k=\chi(G\sqcup H)\) _and let_ \(L\ge 0\) _be an integer. Then_ \(B(G\sqcup H)\le L\) _if and only if_ \(\alpha+\beta\in\mathcal{K}_L(f,g)\) (4.14)

<tbc>_for every_ \(f\in\mathcal{R}_k(G,\unknown)\) _and_ \(g\in\mathcal{R}_k(H,\unknown)\) _whose summed source profile belongs to_ M_<sub>k</sub>(G_)+M_<sub>k</sub>(H). In particular, for L=B(G_)+_B(H), equality_ \(B(G\sqcup H)=B(G)+B(H)\) _holds if and only if this condition holds for every such pair at budget L, and fails for at least one such pair at budget L_-1.

_Proof._ For a fixed pair of responses, \((f\star g)(\mathbf{m})\le L\) means that **m**=**p**+**q** for profiles satisfying \(f(\mathbf{p})+g(\mathbf{q})\le L\). Since costs are integers, this is equivalent to \(\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{K}_L(f,g)\). Theorem 4.9 and (4.13) now give the asserted upper-bound criterion. Failure at _L_-1, together with the bound at _L_, is equivalent to equality. The argument does not require equal chromatic numbers for the summands. □

This is an exact compositional criterion in local profile data, rather than an elementary structural classification of the graph pairs. It distinguishes two effects: target multiplicities may transfer between summands during repair, and a globally feasible disturbance may have locally infeasible profiles.

## 4.4. The growth of ordinary villainy under repetition.

The response composition law also determines the asymptotic behavior of ordinary villainy. Fix a graph _G_ with \(\chi(G)=k\), and let W and P be, respectively, all words and all proper colorings of _G_ on \[_k_\]. Both sets are finite. A vector \(\mathbf{x}=(x_w)_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\) describes proportions of source words on many copies of _G_. Its average profile must belong to the convex hull of the proper profiles. Accordingly, put<tbc>

\(\mathcal{X}_G=\left\{\mathbf{x}\ge\mathbf{0}:\sum_wx_w=1,\sum_wx_w\mathbf{m}(w)\in conv\mathcal{M}_k(G)\right\}.\)

<tbc>For \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_G\), define the fractional repair cost

\(\Phi_G(\mathbf{x})=min_{\mathbf{z}\ge\mathbf{0}}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W},y\in\mathcal{P}}d_\mathrm{H}(w,y)z_{wy},\text{subject to}\sum_yz_{wy}=x_w(w\in\mathcal{W}),\sum_{w,y}z_{wy}(\mathbf{m}(y)-\mathbf{m}(w))=\mathbf{0}.\text{(4.15)}\)

The variable _z<sub>wy</sub>_ assigns a proportion of copies with source _w_ to the proper target _y_. Thus the second constraint preserves the total color counts. The program is feasible precisely for \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_G\). Set<tbc>

\(\Lambda(G)=max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_G}\Phi_G(\mathbf{x}).\) (4.16)

<tbc>**Theorem 4.11** (Ordinary repetition)**.** _For every fixed graph G with_ \(k=\chi(G)\)_, the number_ \(\Lambda(G)\) _is rational and effectively computable. The maximum in_ (4.16) _is attained by a distribution supported on at most k source words, meaning that at most k coordinates x<sub>w</sub> are positive. Moreover,_

\(B(mG)=m\Lambda(G)+O_G(1),\Lambda(G)\ge F_k(G).\) (4.17)

_The error term is bounded by a constant depending only on G. There are effectively computable integers_ \(h\ge 1\), \(a\ge 0\)_, and_ \(M\ge 1\) _such that_ \(a=h\Lambda(G)\) _and_

\(B((m+h)G)=B(mG)+a(m\ge M).\) (4.18)

_Proof._ Write the constraints in (4.15) as _A_**z**=(**x**,**0**), where _A_ is a fixed integer matrix, and write **c** for the nonnegative integer cost vector. When \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^\mathcal{W}\) counts actual source copies, its sum is their number. The source is feasible if and only if the same system has a nonnegative integer solution. In that case the minimum over integer solutions, denoted _C<sub>G</sub>_(**x**), is its ordinary repair cost. This is the repeated form of Theorem 4.9. For unnormalized vectors, we define \(\Phi_G\) by the same program; scaling all source proportions by a nonnegative factor scales its optimum by that factor.

<tbc>For this fixed matrix and cost vector, the integer-programming proximity bound of Cook, Gerards, Schrijver, and Tardos \[4, Corollary 2\] gives a constant _D_, independent of **x**, such that

\(0\le C_G(\mathbf{x})-\Phi_G(\mathbf{x})\le D\) (4.19)

whenever an integer solution exists. To apply that bound, write the equalities as pairs of inequalities and include nonnegativity. The resulting integral constraint matrix and objective are fixed, and the row sums bound every feasible variable.

The function \(\Phi_G\) is convex and piecewise linear by linear programming duality. Its maximum on the rational polytope X_<sub>G</sub>_ is attained at a vertex. Such a vertex has at most _k_ positive coordinates: more than _k_ corresponding profile vectors would be linearly dependent, and a sufficiently small perturbation in that dependence would preserve both the average profile and the sum of the coordinates. Enumerating the vertices and solving the corresponding rational linear programs computes a rational value \(\Lambda(G)\). Any feasible integral source count vector with sum _m_ has \(\mathbf{x}/m\in\mathcal{X}_G\). Thus (4.19) gives \(B(mG)\le m\Lambda(G)+D\).

For the reverse bound, choose a rational maximizer \(\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathcal{X}_G\). Express its average profile as a rational convex combination of proper profiles, and choose a common denominator _d_ for these coefficients and **x**<sup>∗</sup>. Then _d_**x**<sup>∗</sup> is the source count vector of a feasible source on _dG_: the resulting integer numbers of source copies and proper target copies have the same total profile and may be paired arbitrarily. Fix a proper word _y_<sub>0</sub>. For _m=qd+r_, \(0\le r<d\), the integer vector **x**<sup>(_m_)</sup>=_qd_**x**<sup>∗</sup>+_r_**e**<sub>_y_<sub>0</sub></sub> is feasible. Take an optimal dual solution at **x**<sup>∗</sup>, and let **u** denote its coordinates corresponding to the row-sum constraints. Dual feasibility holds for every source count vector, so

\(B(mG)\ge C_G(\mathbf{x}^{(m)})\ge\Phi_G(\mathbf{x}^{(m)})\ge qd\Lambda(G)+ru_{y_0}=m\Lambda(G)-r(\Lambda(G)-u_{y_0}).\)

The final error is bounded independently of _m_, proving the first assertion of (4.17). The second follows from \(B(mG)\ge B_\mathrm{w}(mG)\) and Theorem 4.5.

Finally, the set of pairs (_m,b_) with _b=B(mG_) is definable in Presburger arithmetic, the language of integer linear inequalities and congruences combined by Boolean operations and quantifiers. Indeed, feasible sources, integer repairs, and their costs are described by the fixed linear system above. Let _P(m,t_) assert that some feasible integer source count vector of sum _m_ has every integer repair of cost at least _t_. This is a Presburger formula, and _B(mG_)=_b_ is expressed by \(P(m,b)\wedge\neg P(m,b+1)\). Write \(\Lambda(G)=a_0/h_0\) with integers \(a_0\ge 0\) and \(h_0\ge 1\). After elimination, each linear inequality is eventually constant and each congruence is periodic. Taking a common period _h_ divisible by _h_<sub>0</sub> and a common threshold proves (4.18). The proximity bound and the bound obtained from the dual solution are effective, so the finite set of possible errors can be bounded before applying quantifier elimination. □

Comparing this slope with the fixing-number slope in Theorem 4.5 determines whether the cost of preserving color counts accumulates under repetition.

## 5. Fixed-parameter recognition

The composition laws in Section 4 retain exactly the local information needed for repair, but those data can be large. We now address computation on arbitrary graphs. Small weak villainy forces a small vertex cover in the graph or its complement, so the relevant colorings can be described by boundedly many vertex types.

The classifications of graphs with _B(G_)=0 in \[2\] and with _B(G_)=2 in \[12\] give polynomial- time recognition algorithms for those two classes. We prove the stronger conclusion that recognition is fixed-parameter tractable in the threshold, for both repair rules.

**Theorem 5.1** (Exact computation and recognition)**.** _There are computable functions f,h and an absolute constant c such that both B(G_) _and B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_) _can be computed exactly on an n-vertex graph in time_<tbc>

\(h(B_\mathrm{w}(G))(n+1)^c,\)

<tbc>_without either value being supplied. Moreover, given an integer_ \(t\ge 0\)_, both_

\(\mathrm{min}\{B(G),t+1\}\text{\textit{and}}\mathrm{min}\{B_\mathrm{w}(G),t+1\}\)

_can be computed in time f(t_)(_n_+1)_<sup>c</sup>. Consequently, equality and threshold recognition for either parameter are fixed-parameter tractable in t, and belong to_ P _for every fixed t._

The exponent _c_ is independent of the threshold. The proof first forces a small vertex cover in the graph or its complement, and then uses different descriptions of repair in the two cases. The small-cover case uses effective quantifier elimination; no practical bound on _f_ is asserted. Throughout this section, \(\nu(H)\) denotes the matching number of a graph _H_.

### 5.1. A structural consequence of a matching bound.

For an optimal coloring profile **m**=(_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>k</sub>_), where \(k=\chi(G)\), put

\(p(\mathbf{m})=\sum_{i=1}^k\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{2}\right\rfloor.\)

This is the number of disjoint pairs of equal-colored tokens available in a word of profile **m**. The next lemma extends the matching argument of Jahanbekam and Lin \[12, Lemma 8\].

**Lemma 5.2.** _For every optimal coloring profile_ **m** _of G,_

\(B(G)\ge B_\mathrm{w}(G)\ge\mathrm{min}\{p(\mathbf{m}),\nu(G)\}.\)

_Proof._ Let \(q=\mathrm{min}\{p(\mathbf{m}),\nu(G)\}\). Choose _q_ edges of a matching and _q_ disjoint pairs of equal- colored tokens. Place each pair at the ends of one chosen edge and distribute the remaining tokens arbitrarily. The resulting word has profile **m**. Every proper coloring differs from it at an endpoint of each of the _q_ selected edges. The edges are disjoint, so these discrepancies occur at distinct vertices. This argument does not require the repaired coloring to have profile **m**, and therefore proves the bound for _B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_). □

The matching bound forces a graph of small weak villainy to have either a small vertex cover or very many colors. In the latter case, the complement has a small vertex cover instead.

**Corollary 5.3.** _If_ \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le t\)_, then_

\(\nu(G)\le t\text{\textit{or}}\chi(G)\ge n-2t.\)

_In the first case G has a vertex cover of size at most_ 2_t. In the second case_ \(\nu(\overline{G})\le 2t\)_, and <o>G</o> has a vertex cover of size at most_ 4_t. The same conclusions hold if_ \(B(G)\le t\).

_Proof._ Fix an optimal profile **m**. Since every _m<sub>i</sub>_ is positive,

\(n-\chi(G)=\sum_i(m_i-1)\le 2\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{2}\right\rfloor=2p(\mathbf{m}).\)

If \(\nu(G)>t\), Theorem 5.2 forces \(p(\mathbf{m})\le t\), and hence \(\chi(G)\ge n-2t\).

<tbc>The endpoints of a maximum matching form a vertex cover: otherwise an edge with both endpoints uncovered could be added to the matching. This gives the first cover bound. Moreover, a matching of size _q_ in <o>_G_</o> supplies _q_ disjoint nonadjacent pairs in _G_. Giving each pair one color and every remaining vertex its own color gives \(\chi(G)\le n-q\). Thus \(\nu(\overline{G})\le n-\chi(G)\le 2t\) in the second case, and the same endpoint argument gives its cover bound. Finally, \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le B(G)\). □

## 5.2. Descriptions of colorings by types.

Let \(U\subseteq V(G)\), with |_U_|=_s_, and suppose that _V(G_)\\_U_ is either an independent set or a clique. For a vertex \(v\notin U\), define its type to be \(\tau(v)=N_G(v)\cap U\). Write \(V_\tau\) for the vertices of type \(\tau\) and \(n_\tau=|V_\tau|\), keeping only nonempty types. There are at most 2_<sup>s</sup>_ types. Any permutation fixing _U_ pointwise and preserving each \(V_\tau\) is an automorphism of _G_; let \(\Gamma\) be the group of these permutations.

For a finite label set _L_, describe a map \(x:V(G)\rightarrow L\) by its restriction to _U_, called its _core map_, and by the vectors

\(\mathbf{x}_\tau=(x_{\tau i})_{i\in L},x_{\tau i}=|V_\tau\cap x^{-1}(i)|.\)

Two maps have the same description if and only if an element of \(\Gamma\) takes one to the other. The next observation is the reason that descriptions can replace individual words in a repair problem.

**Lemma 5.4.** _Let_ A _and_ C _be descriptions of maps_ \(x,y:V(G)\rightarrow L\)_. Define_

\(\delta(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})=|\{u\in U:x(u)\neq y(u)\}|+\sum_\tau\left(n_\tau-\sum_{i\in L}\mathrm{min}\{x_{\tau i},y_{\tau i}\}\right).\)

_For every fixed realization x of_ A_, this is the minimum Hamming distance from x to a realization of_ C.

_Proof._ The labels on _U_ are fixed. In \(V_\tau\), at most \(\mathrm{min}\{x_{\tau i},y_{\tau i}\}\) vertices can receive label _i_ in both maps. These upper bounds can be achieved simultaneously: for each _i_, match that many occurrences of _i_ in _y_ to occurrences of _i_ in the fixed map _x_, and then biject the remaining positions arbitrarily. Such bijections can be chosen independently in each type. The displayed formula follows by subtracting the maximum number of agreements from _n_. □

In particular, if a collection of permitted repairs is invariant under \(\Gamma\), the minimum repair distance depends only on the description of the disturbed word. The minimum is computed by minimizing \(\delta\) over the descriptions of permitted repairs.

## 5.3. Graphs with a small vertex cover.

**Proposition 5.5.** _Given a vertex cover U of size s, the values B(G_) _and B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_) _can be computed in time g(s_)(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>_, for a computable function g._

_Proof._ Put _I=V(G_)\\_U_. Since _I_ is independent, \(k=\chi(G)\le s+1\). We first compute _k_. For each _j_=1_,...,s_+1, enumerate the proper maps \(\varphi:U\rightarrow[j]\). Such a map extends to a proper _j_-coloring of _G_ if and only if each nonempty type \(\tau\) has a color outside \(\varphi(\tau)\). Indeed, all vertices of a type can be assigned any one such color. The first successful value of _j_ is _k_.

Direct enumeration of the type counts would give an exponent depending on _s_. Instead, we express the threshold condition by a short formula in Presburger arithmetic: integer linear inequalities and congruences with fixed coefficients, combined by Boolean operations and quantifiers. Effective quantifier elimination converts such a formula into an equivalent quantifier-free one. We use this established result, not its quantitative refinements; see Haase et al. \[11, Corollary 3.2\]. Universal quantifiers can be eliminated by negation.

Include all 2_<sup>s</sup>_ types, including empty ones. Introduce free variables \(\mathbf{N}=(N_\tau)_{\tau\subseteq U}\) for their sizes and a free threshold variable \(\ell\). These variables are not yet assigned their input values.

For an integer array \(\mathbf{x}=(x_{\tau i})\) and a map \(a:U\rightarrow[k]\), use the following predicates and linear forms: \(R(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{N}):x_{\tau i}\ge 0\text{for all}\tau,i,\sum_ix_{\tau i}=N_\tau\text{for all}\tau,\)
\(P_a(\mathbf{x}):a\text{is proper on}G[U],x_{\tau i}=0\text{whenever}i\in a(\tau),\)
\(\mu_i(a,\mathbf{x})=|a^{-1}(i)|+\sum_\tau x_{\tau i}.\) Here properness of the fixed map _a_ is a Boolean constant. The first predicate says that **x** describes a word; adding the second says that the word is proper. Write \(\mu(a,\mathbf{x})=(\mu_i(a,\mathbf{x}))_{i=1}^k\). Let \(c,a:U\rightarrow[k]\) represent, respectively, an original coloring and a disturbance. The predicate \(A_{c,a}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},\mathbf{N}):R(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{N})\wedge P_c(\mathbf{x})\wedge R(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{N})\)
\(\wedge\mu(c,\mathbf{x})=\mu(a,\mathbf{z})\) says that the disturbed description (_a,_**z**) has a feasible profile, witnessed by the proper description (_c,_**x**). For a target map \(b:U\rightarrow[k]\), put \(d_U(a,b)=|\{u\in U:a(u)\neq b(u)\}|\). Define \(T_{a,b}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h};\mathbf{N},\ell)\) by the conjunction of \(R(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{N}),P_b(\mathbf{y}),\mu(b,\mathbf{y})=\mu(a,\mathbf{z}),\)
\(0\le h_{\tau i}\le z_{\tau i},h_{\tau i}\le y_{\tau i}\text{for every}\tau,i,\)
\(d_U(a,b)+\sum_\tau N_\tau-\sum_{\tau,i}h_{\tau i}\le\ell.\) By Theorem 5.4, this predicate has witnesses **y**,**h** exactly when a same-profile proper target with core map _b_ is within distance \(\ell\). Indeed, the greatest possible total agreement in each type is \(\sum_imin\{z_{\tau i},y_{\tau i}\}\), and is attainable for every fixed realization of the source. The variables \(h_{\tau i}\) encode these agreements using only linear constraints. Let \(\Psi_a(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{N},\ell)\) abbreviate \(\vee_{b:U\rightarrow[k]}\exists\mathbf{y}\exists\mathbf{h}T_{a,b}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h};\mathbf{N},\ell)\). Consider the formula \(\Phi(\mathbf{N},\ell)=\wedge_{c,a:U\rightarrow[k]}\forall\mathbf{x}\forall\mathbf{z}(A_{c,a}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},\mathbf{N})\Longrightarrow\Psi_a(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{N},\ell)).\) (5.1) All quantified arrays range over the integers. After substituting \(N_\tau=n_\tau\), this formula holds precisely when \(B(G)\le\ell\). Every admissible disturbance has at least one proper profile witness, so the implication requires a repair for it. A disturbance with an infeasible profile has no such witness and imposes no condition. Although the witness is universally quantified, the permitted repairs depend only on the disturbance, not on which witness was used. For weak villainy, delete the profile equality from _Ta,b_ only; the source-feasibility predicate _Ac,a_ is unchanged. The resulting formula is equivalent to \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\le\ell\). Both formulas have length bounded by a function of _s_: there are \(k\le s+1\) colors, 2_s_ types, and at most _k_2_s_ pairs of core maps. All coefficients and core constants are bounded in _s_. Crucially, **N** and \(\ell\) remain free during quantifier elimination. Thus the elimination time, the output length, and its coefficient lengths are bounded by a computable function of _s_, independently of the numerical type sizes. Substituting their actual values and evaluating the resulting formula takes _g(s_)(log(_n_+1))_O_(1) time. This is a uniform algorithm: the formulas are generated from the given graph on _U_ and then processed by an effective elimination procedure. Binary search on \(0\le\ell\le n\), together with input processing, computes both values in the claimed time. □ ## 5.4. Graphs with a small complement cover. Suppose next that _W=V(G_)\\_U_ is a clique. The chromatic number need not be bounded, but its computation still depends on only a bounded part of the graph.

<tbc>**Lemma 5.6.** _If_ |_U_|=_s and V(G_)\\_U is a clique, then_ \(\chi(G)\) _can be computed in time_ 2<sup>_O(s_log(_s_+2))</sup>(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>.

_Proof._ Enumerate the partitions \(\pi\) of _U_ into independent sets. In any proper coloring inducing \(\pi\), a vertex of _W_ either has a color not used on _U_, or shares a color with one part of \(\pi\). No two vertices of _W_ can share a color. Thus the possible sharing is described by a matching in the bipartite graph whose sides are \(\pi\) and _W_, with a part adjacent to \(v\in W\) when _v_ has no neighbor in that part. If a maximum matching has size \(a(\pi)\), the fewest colors for this partition are

\(|\pi|+|W|-a(\pi).\)

Taking the minimum over \(\pi\) gives \(\chi(G)\). There are at most _s<sup>s</sup>_ partitions for \(s\ge 1\), and each matching is computed in polynomial time. The empty partition handles _s_=0. □

We shall use the following elementary fact to handle the many singleton color classes. It does not depend on the structure of _G_.

**Lemma 5.7.** _Let_ \(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}'\) _be positive profiles on_ \[_k_\] _of the same total size, and suppose that G admits a proper coloring of profile_ \(\mathbf{m}'\)_. Let_ \(J\subseteq[k]\) _contain every color having multiplicity at least two in either profile. Replace each color outside J by a common label_ ∗_. For a fixed word w of profile_ **m**_, the minimum Hamming distance to a proper coloring of profile_ \(\mathbf{m}'\) _equals the minimum Hamming distance between the resulting label maps._

_Proof._ Different labels imply different colors, so passing to labels can only decrease a distance. To prove the reverse inequality, take any proper coloring _y_ of profile \(\mathbf{m}'\) and let _R<sub>w</sub>,R<sub>y</sub>_ be the positions with label ∗ in the two maps. Both restrictions to the star positions are bijections onto the same color set _S_=\[_k_\]\\_J_, since every color in _S_ has multiplicity one in both profiles.

Keep the colors of _y_ outside _R<sub>y</sub>_. On \(R_w\cap R_y\), assign the colors of _w_. Fill _R<sub>y</sub>_\\_R<sub>w</sub>_ bijectively with the unused colors in _S_. This preserves the target profile and properness: all changed color classes are singletons. It also makes the two colorings agree at every position at which their label maps agree. Consequently its Hamming distance from _w_ is exactly the label distance of the original pair. Minimizing proves the assertion. □

We can now combine the type description with Theorem 5.7: only the colors occurring more than once need individual names. The resulting count is controlled by the size of the cover and by the difference between the order and chromatic number.

**Proposition 5.8.** _Suppose that_ \(|U|\le s\), _V(G_)\\_U is a clique, and_ \(n-\chi(G)\le e\)_. Then both B(G_) _and B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_) _can be computed in time f(s,e_)(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>_, for a computable function f. One may take_<tbc>

\(f(s,e)=2^{O(se+(s+e)log(s+e+2))}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Compute \(k=\chi(G)\) by Theorem 5.6, and put \(d=n-k\le e\). For every positive profile **m** on \[_k_\],<tbc>

\(\sum_i(m_i-1)=d.\)

<tbc>Consequently its set _N_ of nonsingular colors has size at most _d_, and

\(\sum_{i\in N}m_i=d+|N|\le 2e.\)

Up to a permutation of color names, there are only a bounded number of such profiles: their nonsingular excesses _m<sub>i</sub>_-1 form a partition of _d_. A _profile shape_ is a profile considered up to a permutation of color names. We enumerate these shapes, choose a labeled representative of each, and discard it if it is not the profile of a proper coloring. The properness test is included in the description enumeration below. A simultaneous permutation of color names preserves repair distances, so these representatives suffice for the outer maximum in both parameters.

First consider _B(G_) and fix one such profile **m**. Use labels \(N\cup\{*\}\), with ∗ replacing singleton colors. The nonsingular labels occupy at most 2_e_ vertices. For a label map to come<tbc>

<tbc>from a proper coloring, the vertices assigned each nonstar label must form an independent set. This can be checked from the description: its vertices in _U_ must be independent, the label may occur at most once in the clique _W_, and any such vertex must have a type disjoint from that label’s vertex set in _U_. The star positions impose no constraint, because they receive distinct singleton colors. We retain only descriptions having total count _m<sub>i</sub>_ for every \(i\in N\) and total star count _k_-|_N_|, for both sources and targets.

By Theorem 5.7, the distance to a best repair of the same profile is exactly the distance to a best proper label map. By Theorem 5.4, this minimum, and then the maximum over disturbed words, can be evaluated using descriptions alone. The number of descriptions is bounded by a function of _s,e_. For example, after choosing the at most (_e_+1)_<sup>s</sup>_ labels on _U_, the at most 2_e_ nonstar occurrences outside _U_ are distributed among at most _e_2_<sup>s</sup>_ label-type pairs. An overcount is

\((e+1)^s(e2^s+1)^{2e}.\)

Star counts are then determined by the type sizes. Testing all descriptions and comparing all pairs proves the first running-time bound.

For weak villainy, the target may have a different profile. Here the choice of target nonsingleton colors must be made after the disturbed word has been fixed. We describe this order explicitly. For each source description using labels \(N\cup\{*\}\), choose one full-color representative _w_, assigning the source singleton colors bijectively to its star positions. All words represented by this reduced description have the same weak repair distance. Indeed, two such words are related by an automorphism in \(\Gamma\) followed by a permutation of singleton color names that fixes _N_. Both transformations preserve Hamming distances and the set of proper _k_-colorings.

With _w_ fixed, let \(N'\) be the nonsingleton colors of a target. Colors in \(N'\backslash N\) are singleton in the source; call them _promoted colors_. Each is identified by its unique position in _w_. Enumerating their names separately would introduce a factor depending on _n_ with exponent _e_. We avoid this by using symmetries that fix the full source word.

Let \(\gamma\in\Gamma\) permute only source-star positions within each outside type, fixing all other vertices. Define a color permutation \(\pi_\gamma\) by \(\pi_\gamma(w(v))=w(\gamma(v))\) on source singleton colors, and fix every color in _N_. For any target coloring _y_, put

\((T_\gamma y)(v)=\pi_\gamma\big(y(\gamma^{-1}(v))\big).\)

Then \(T_\gamma w=w\). Moreover, \(T_\gamma\) preserves properness and Hamming distance, because \(\gamma\) is a graph automorphism and \(\pi_\gamma\) is a permutation of colors. In particular, \(d_\mathrm{H}(w,T_\gamma y)=d_\mathrm{H}(w,y)\).

These transformations act transitively on choices of promoted colors that occupy the same source singleton positions in _U_ and have the same number of source positions in each outside type. Consequently, we need only choose a subset of the source singleton positions in _U_, and integers \(h_\tau\ge 0\) with \(\sum_\tau h_\tau\le e\), not exceeding the available number of source-star positions of type \(\tau\). For each choice, fix one set of \(h_\tau\) singleton names from that type. There are at most 2_<sup>s</sup>_(2_<sup>s</sup>_+1)_<sup>e</sup>_ such choices: the count vectors are overcounted by sequences of _e_ type names or unused slots. Choose also the subset \(N'\cap N\), and retain only sets with \(|N'|\le d\). For each resulting \(N'\), enumerate every assignment

\(m'_i\ge 2(i\in N'),m'_i=1(i\notin N'),\sum_{i\in N^\prime}(m'_i-1)=d.\)

Every target is equivalent, under a transformation fixing _w_, to one of these choices. Its excesses are carried along by the color permutation and occur in the enumeration. For each choice, use the label set \(J\cup\{*\}\) with \(J=N\cup N'\). The star label now represents exactly the colors that are singleton in both profiles. Theorem 5.7 applies to this fixed source and target profile, and Theorem 5.4 computes the minimum over proper target descriptions. Colors in \(N'\backslash N\) have one source occurrence, and colors in \(N\backslash N'\) have one target occurrence; these occurrences retain their individual labels. Thus no potential agreement is lost by the reduction. Each target description must have total count \(m'_i\) for \(i\in J\) and exactly _k_-|_J_| star positions; target profiles with no proper description are discarded.

<tbc>There are at most 2<sup>_s+e_</sup>(2_<sup>s</sup>_+1)_<sup>e</sup>_ choices of \(N'\), and a number depending only on _e_ of assignments of its positive excesses. Each map on the union label set has at most 3_e_ nonstar occurrences and at most 2_e_ nonstar labels. Its descriptions are therefore bounded in number by

\((2e+1)^s(2e2^s+1)^{3e}.\)

Minimize over the target profiles and descriptions for this fixed _w_, then maximize over source descriptions and admissible source profile shapes. The order of these operations is exactly the order in Theorem 2.2. This proves the second running-time bound. The displayed description and orbit bounds, the number of profile shapes, and Theorem 5.6 give the stated choice of _f(s,e_), with the cases _e_=0 interpreted directly. □

### 5.5. The recognition algorithm.

_Proof of Theorem 5.1._ Fix _t_. If _G_ is empty, return zero for both parameters. Otherwise, compute a maximum matching in _G_. If its size is at most _t_, its endpoints form a vertex cover of size at most 2_t_. Theorem 5.5 computes both parameters exactly; truncate each answer at _t_+1.

Otherwise \(\nu(G)>t\). Compute a maximum matching in <o>_G_</o>. If \(\nu(\overline{G})>2t\), then \(\chi(G)\le n-\nu(\overline{G})<n-2t\). Theorem 5.3 implies _B_<sub>w</sub>(_G)\>t_, and hence also _B(G)\>t_. Return _t_+1 for both parameters.

In the remaining case, the endpoints of a maximum matching in <o>_G_</o> give a set _U_ of size at most 4_t_ whose complement is a clique in _G_. Compute \(\chi(G)\) using Theorem 5.6. If \(\chi(G)<n-2t\), the same dichotomy again gives both answers as _t_+1. If \(\chi(G)\ge n-2t\), apply Theorem 5.8 with \(s\le 4t\) and \(e\le 2t\), and truncate the exact answers at _t_+1.

This exhausts all graphs and proves correctness. By Theorem 5.5, the first branch takes time _g_(2_t_)(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>, after replacing _g_ by a nondecreasing computable bound if necessary. By Theorem 5.8, the complement-cover branch takes time 2<sup>_O_((_t_+1)<sup>2</sup>)</sup>(_n_+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>. Input processing and matching computations add only fixed polynomial factors. Their exponents are independent of _t_, proving the stated bound with a computable _f_. The argument includes _t_=0.

To obtain the exact values with weak villainy as parameter, run this structural algorithm at thresholds 0,1,2,4_,..._. Whenever an exact-computation branch is reached, retain both answers before truncation and stop. Continue only after a rejection, which certifies _B_<sub>w</sub>(_G)\>t_. By Theorem 5.3, rejection is impossible once \(t\ge B_\mathrm{w}(G)\). If \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)\ge 1\), the largest tested threshold is at most 2_B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_); if it is zero, the first run succeeds. Taking a nondecreasing envelope of the parameter bounds and absorbing the number of runs proves the claim. □

**Corollary 5.9.** _Unless_ P=NP_, there is no fixed integer t for which recognition of B(G_)=_t is NP-complete. The same conclusion holds for B_<sub>w</sub>(_G_)=_t._

## 6. Concluding remarks and questions

The composition laws quantify how global color counts couple components. For repeated copies, Theorems 4.6 and 4.11 give effective eventual formulas for both repair rules. Their slopes also decide whether the difference between the two values stays bounded. The next questions ask for structural descriptions and sharper bounds than the finite local optimizations provide.

**Problem 6.1.** Find structural or efficiently checkable versions of the criteria in Theorems 4.4 and 4.10. In particular, characterize the graphs satisfying \(B_\mathrm{w}(G)=F_{\chi(G)}(G)\), equivalently those for which weak villainy is additive over every repetition.

For either parameter _F_, the _superadditivity deficit_ is \(F(G)+F(H)-F(G\sqcup H)\); a positive value measures a failure of superadditivity.

<tbc>**Problem 6.2.** Determine sharp bounds on the superadditivity deficits at prescribed orders and chromatic numbers. For weak villainy, the unresolved deficit case has unequal chromatic numbers. Give a structural characterization of the graphs satisfying \(\Lambda(G)=F_{\chi(G)}(G)\), the finite optimization criterion for bounded difference in Theorem 4.12.

The explicit stabilization bound in Theorem 4.6 comes from a general zero-sum estimate and need not be sharp.

**Problem 6.3.** Determine sharp bounds on the least stabilization index for weak repetition, meaning the least index from which the eventual periodic formula holds, and give graph- theoretic descriptions of its least period. Obtain comparable explicit bounds for the ordinary recurrence in Theorem 4.11.

The odd-cycle theorem of \[13, Theorem 3.15\] already gives singleton response families on a three-color palette, as discussed after Theorem 4.9.

**Problem 6.4.** For a fixed palette size, determine further graph classes whose response families in Theorem 4.9 admit polynomial-size representations supporting polynomial-time composition and queries. How much can these families be compressed without changing ordinary villainy after any further disjoint union?

The parameter dependence in Theorem 5.1 comes from general-purpose quantifier elimination. Can both values be computed by a direct combinatorial algorithm in time 2<sup>_B_w(_G_)<sup>_O_(1)</sup></sup>(|_V(G_)|+1)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>?
